complice.endingText:
1919. Whitehall, London.

You have an office with a window. A small window, true, but the door has your name on a polished brass plate: MAJ. EDMUND VALE, DEPT. OF SPECIAL OPERATIONS. No one knows what the department does. You do not really know either — you only know what you sign.

Twice a week, someone hands you a manila folder. You read. You sign. You return it. You never discuss. You never ask. Someone in another office opens the next folder based on what you signed. That is how it works.

Petrov died of tuberculosis in Marseille, 1920. Wren went back to Oxford, wrote a medical paper on “combat fatigue” no one published. Ashcroft vanished — the files say “transferred to continental operation”. Wardell writes once a year, on the anniversary of the Armistice. You reply once every two.

You still look yourself in the eye in the mirror. You still sleep without dreams. Your wife is kind and does not ask about work. Your children go up to Oxford in 1938.

Someone has to do the work you do. You accepted that. And the work, whatever it is, continues to be done.

You are not unhappy. You are not happy either. You are useful.

That will have to be enough.

contentor.endingText:
1919. Yorkshire.

Your family home is exactly as you left it in 1914. Your mother has aged. Your father died in 1917 and you never got leave for the funeral. You stay in the room that was yours, now a bit too small for the adult you have become.

You do not speak of the war. No one asks twice.

In the garden there is a small stone where no one is buried, but you leave a flower there every week. Your mother asks once. You say it is for the friends who did not come back. She does not ask again. She knows you are lying, but she also knows the lie does you good.

You accept a teaching post at the primary school. You teach ancient history to boys of twelve. You look after them with a care the other teachers find excessive. You know a few things about what can enter the world through the margins, if no one is careful.

You never tell anyone what Krüger said before he died. What the Apostle whispered. What the General showed. You carry it all. You keep it under your tongue like a child keeps a small stone — so that when someone tries to make you speak, you remember there is something heavy and cold in there that must stay put.

You lived until 1962. Seventy-two years. Never spoke to anyone about what you did, what you saw, what you carried.

Someone had to carry it. It was you. It is done.

testemunha.endingText:
1919-1958. Various addresses.

You did not go back to Yorkshire. You did not go back to Oxford. You rent a room in Bloomsbury and write. You write for 39 years.

The first book comes out in 1923 and is ignored. The second in 1927, the same. The third — “On Recurring Patterns in Armed Conflict: 1848-1918” — comes out in 1931, gets two good reviews and sells 84 copies. You do not give up.

You travel. Rennes, Prague, Alexandria, a village near Kholm that no longer exists. You interview survivors. You catalogue sigils. You draw maps. You consult archives no one should ever have let you consult.

In the 1940s, you predict certain things. No one listens. You continue documenting. In the 1950s, a few young men begin to seek you out. Students from small universities. Amateurs. You tell them everything. They take notes.

You die in 1958 in a boarding-house room in Camden. The landlord finds thirty-four boxes of archives and five decades of correspondence. One of the young men — an American named Perry — inherits it all, because he is the one left to ask.

Perry will publish in 1971. The book will be discredited in 1972. It will be reissued in 1998. Someone in 2024 will read the reissued version and will recognise the pattern in something that happened near her. She will begin to document.

You do not know it, but the chain continues. You were a link. Someone had to be.

fugitivo.endingText:
1919. West coast of Scotland.

You gave up everything. Changed names twice. You live in a cottage near a lighthouse where no one asks anything. You work as assistant to the old lighthouse keeper. He teaches you to clean the crystal lens, to douse the mechanism, to wait.

You write to no one. You receive no correspondence. You do not read the papers. Your mother dies in 1924 believing you vanished in combat. Your friends assume the same. No one searches for long — the war left millions missing, and you are only one more.

At night, when the lighthouse turns, you sit on the porch with a pipe you almost never light. You look at the sea. You listen to the wind. You think of nothing in particular. If a thought begins to turn into an image — of Krüger, of the Apostle, of the General — you stand up and make tea. That almost always works.

You lived that way for 42 years. The old keeper died in 1932. You took over the post. A few more keepers passed through here, all old too, and you taught them what you had learned.

You died in 1961 in the same room, of no particular illness, only of age. You were buried in the village cemetery, under the false name.

No one knows where you are. That was the thing you wanted.

You succeeded.

espelho.endingText:
1919. Psychiatric infirmary, Ward 12.

You wake in a hospital bed. A nurse comes in. She smiles with pity.

“Good morning, Henry. Did you take your medicine?”

You look at her. Open your mouth to correct her — I am not Henry, I am Edmund, my brother died at Loos in 1915 — but your mouth will not obey.

You look at your hands. You know they are your own. You know they always were.

You are Henry Vale. You have always been Henry Vale.

Edmund died at Loos with you, 1915. Only you did not die. You came back. And since then you have invented everything — the Salvage Corps, Petrov, Wren, Ashcroft, Krüger, the Apostle, the General. A whole war inside your head. Because the alternative was sitting in a white room in silence, thinking of your brother's face.

The nurse helps you sit up. You take the medicine.

Tomorrow you will begin again. You will go back to being Lieutenant Edmund Vale. You will face Krüger again, the Apostle again, the General again. You will make different choices perhaps. You will arrive here again, at the mirror, at your own face.

It is the only way you found to keep existing.

It is all right.
